history: School started as free time. Greek skholḗ meant ‘leisure’, the time a free man did not have to work. Some spent it in discussion and learning, so the word moved from the free time to the lecture and then to the place where it happened. Latin borrowed it as schola. Portuguese, like Spanish, cannot begin a word with s plus a consonant, so it added a vowel in front: schola became escola, just as Latin spiritus became espírito and stella became estrela. Portuguese speakers learning English often do the same and say ‘eschool’. Today Portuguese children go to a escola primária or a escola secundária, and a driving school is an escola de condução.
historyEinfach: Escola means ‘school’. The word comes from Greek skholḗ, ‘free time’. People used their free time to talk and learn. Latin took the word: schola. Portuguese puts an e before s + consonant, so schola became escola. English school comes from the same word.

elsewhere.text: English took the Latin word early and kept the s at the start.
Spanish also added the e, and then broke the o into ue.
